items.q: The deck says **"CRM is not just about technology."** What else does it involve?
options: Strategy and redesign of business processes
A larger sales team and more field visits
A dedicated data warehouse and BI licence
Outsourcing the call centre
items.explain:
**"It involves strategy and redesign of business processes."**

**This is exactly Unit 2's argument about ERP itself:** buying the software achieves nothing unless the underlying processes change. **A company that installs a CRM but keeps its sales people hoarding contacts in personal notebooks has bought a database nobody fills in.**

**ERP without BPR fails; CRM without process redesign fails — for the same reason.**

items.q: CRM's stated goal is a four-stage life cycle. Which is it?
options: Find, attract and win new customers · retain them · get feedback to better design products and processes
Advertise · sell · invoice · collect
Segment · target · position · measure
Acquire · configure · deliver · support
items.explain:
$$\textbf{find} \rightarrow \textbf{attract and win} \rightarrow \textbf{retain} \rightarrow \textbf{learn from}$$

**The application areas are that life cycle with software attached** — Marketing finds, SFA wins, Call Centre and Field Service retain, CRM Analytics learns.

**The last stage is the one people forget.** *"Getting feedback… to better design the company's product and customer facing processes"* means **CRM is an input to product design** — which is what makes it a *strategy* rather than a sales tool.

items.q: Put the sales funnel stages in order.
options: Leads → Prospects → Opportunities → Customer → Account → Repeat Sales
Prospects → Leads → Customer → Opportunities → Account
Contacts → Leads → Accounts → Opportunities → Customer
Opportunities → Leads → Prospects → Account → Customer
items.explain:
**A sequence of increasing commitment:** a **lead** is a name; a **prospect** is a *qualified* lead; an **opportunity** is a specific potential sale with a value and close date; a **customer** has a **Sales Order**; an **account** is an ongoing relationship where support tickets are **cases**.

**The Customer → Account transition is where CRM stops being about selling** — the goal changes from *win* to *retain*. **That is the boundary between the sales applications and the service applications.**

items.q: Which are typical areas of **Sales Force Automation**? *(select all that apply)*
options: Contact management
Lead / Opportunity management
Territory management and sales performance management
Campaign management and loyalty marketing
items.explain:
Plus **sales forecasting and pipeline** and **quote generation**. ⚠️ **Option D is Marketing Management**, not SFA.

**The most important consequence is stated obliquely:** *"tracking sales performance, based on which they are provided **incentive / compensation**."*

> **That is why salespeople actually use the system.** An SFA that only helps management see the pipeline gets filled in badly; **one that computes commission gets filled in accurately and on time.**

items.q: Which capability of a **call centre application** does the question bank single out as most valuable, and what delivers it?
options: Previous records of the caller — delivered by CTI, which opens the record as the phone rings
Predefined escalation route — delivered by ACD
Knowledge base — delivered by IVR
Self-service capability — delivered by web integration
items.explain:
**Without it, every call starts from zero** — the customer re-explains their problem to a third person, and the company appears not to be one company. **It is the single customer view arriving in the two seconds before the agent says hello.**

**CTI = Computer Technology Integration** — it links the telephone system to the customer database so the screen and the call arrive together.

*(The eight capabilities: predefined escalation route · previous records · time zones and languages · managing call assignments · knowledge base · self service · workflow · field service management.)*

items.q: What does a call-centre **knowledge base** ultimately enable?
options: Self-service — once a solution is written down, any agent can reuse it, and it can then be exposed to customers directly
Automatic call distribution to the least busy agent
Voice logging for compliance
Multi-language support
items.explain:
$$\textbf{one agent solves it} \rightarrow \textbf{knowledge base} \rightarrow \textbf{every agent solves it} \rightarrow \textbf{self-service: the customer solves it}$$

**Each arrow removes cost and reduces waiting.**

**Same principle as ESS in HCM and employee e-procurement for indirect items:** *move the transaction to the person who has the need.*

items.q: In **field service**, four constraints must all be satisfied for a visit to succeed. Which are they?
options: Skill, availability, location and the right spare part on the van
Skill, cost, contract level and warranty status
Availability, language, seniority and territory
Location, vehicle capacity, route and fuel
items.explain:
**Any three can be satisfied while the fourth fails — and the visit still achieves nothing.** An engineer with the skill, the time and the location but **not the part** has to come back tomorrow, doubling the cost.

**That is why "managing spares / service parts" sits in a customer-relationship module** — the inventory is **distributed across vans**, and the service level it supports is **first-time fix rate**.

**And "reverse logistics" is the distinctive direction:** the faulty part must come **back**.

items.q: Why does **PRM** exist as a separate application from CRM?
options: Because the partner is an independent business you cannot instruct — you can only make it attractive for them to sell your product
Because partners require a different database technology
Because partner data is subject to different privacy law
Because partners buy at wholesale rather than retail prices
items.explain:
| | **Direct selling (CRM)** | **Channel selling (PRM)** |
|---|---|---|
| Who meets the customer | **your** salesperson | **the partner's** |
| Who controls them | you — employees | **nobody** — independent business |

**Every PRM capability is a lever:** distributing leads · special partner discounts · partner training and service · partner performance management.

⚠️ **"Managing channel inventory" is the hardest and most valuable** — **sold to the channel ≠ sold to the customer**, and mistaking channel stocking for real demand is how the **bullwhip effect** starts.

items.q: Which type of CRM analytics is described as using **predictive analytics**?
options: Marketing analytics — for customer segmentation, targeting and campaign ROI
Sales analytics — dashboards displaying KPIs
Customer service analytics — visibility into call centre performance
All three equally
items.explain:
**Only marketing analytics is described as predictive**, and that is not accidental: **marketing must commit budget in advance of knowing the outcome**, so a prediction has direct value. Sales analytics reports on deals that already exist; service analytics watches a queue already forming.

**"Measure the effectiveness (ROI) of a campaign" is the thing CRM makes possible that was previously impossible** — *half of advertising is wasted and nobody knows which half* is a **measurement** problem.

items.q: In the deck's **2018 CRM vendor quadrant**, which vendors are the Leaders?
options: Pipedrive, HubSpot, Salesforce, Zoho
SAP, Oracle, Microsoft, Adobe
Oracle CRM On Demand, amoCRM, Gold-Vision, Bpm'online
Highrise, Base, Hatchbuck, Vtiger
items.explain:
The quadrant plots **Value Score** against **Capability Score**: **Leaders** *(high both)* · **Masters** *(high value, lower capability)* · **Pacesetters** *(high capability, lower value)* · **Contenders**.

⚠️ **Oracle CRM On Demand is a Pacesetter** — capable but judged expensive for what it delivers, which is exactly what *"Price and **Value** for Money"* meant as a criterion.

> **Salesforce leading rather than SAP or Oracle is the whole story** — CRM is where the specialists beat the suites, because it sits at the **edge** of the enterprise and needs far less core integration.

items.q: **PLM** manages product data from when to when, and why is it described as cross-functional?
options: From initial conception to retirement — because R&D, Engineering, Marketing, Production, Quality, Sales and Service all touch the product
From design release to first shipment — because engineering and manufacturing must agree
From order to delivery — because sales and logistics must coordinate
From patent filing to expiry — because legal and R&D must coordinate
items.explain:
*"PLM manages all data and information about a product **from its initial conception to retirement**"*, and **PLM processes are cross functional — R&D, Engineering, Marketing, Production, Quality, Sales and Service.**

$$\textbf{one product} \times \textbf{seven functions} \Rightarrow \textbf{seven partial views, unless something unifies them}$$

**PLM is to a *product* what HCM is to an *employee* and CRM is to a *customer*** — the same architectural idea, three times.

items.q: Which are stated **business drivers for a PLM application**? *(select all that apply)*
options: Product variants and growing product lines
Shorter product development cycles and reduced engineering resources
Regulatory compliance pressure and documentation control
Falling raw material prices
items.explain:
Plus **cost reduction pressure · collaboration with local and global partners · process and data integration between R&D, Production, Supply · innovation focus · intellectual asset management**.

**The first group is a squeeze from both ends and is the strongest argument for PLM:** more variants, more products, less time, **fewer engineers**. **Those four cannot all be satisfied by working harder** — the only way is to stop re-designing what already exists, which requires knowing what exists.

⚠️ *(The source list repeats "product variants and growing product lines" at both ends — treat it as **ten distinct drivers**.)*

items.q: What is the difference between an **EBOM** and an **MBOM**, and why does it matter to PLM?
options: EBOM is structured by function as engineering designs it; MBOM by assembly sequence as the factory needs it, including packaging and consumables — PLM owns the engineering side and hands over to ERP
EBOM is the estimated BOM; MBOM is the measured BOM after production
EBOM covers electronics; MBOM covers mechanical parts
EBOM is a draft; MBOM is the approved version of the same list
items.explain:
**EBOM ≠ MBOM, and reconciling them is a real problem in practice.**

That handover is the honest answer to *"what are the differences of a PLM application from an ERP application?"* — **PLM manages the product *before and around* it is made; ERP manages *making and selling* it.** PLM's world is designs, revisions, documents and approvals; ERP's is orders, stock, costs and postings. **The BOM is where they meet**, and the same part carries **one identity in design and another in production**.

items.q: What are the **five basic components** of the SCOR model?
options: Plan, Source, Make, Deliver, Return
Plan, Buy, Build, Ship, Bill
Forecast, Procure, Produce, Distribute, Service
Source, Store, Move, Sell, Support
items.explain:
**SCOR = Supply Chain Operational Reference.** The diagram draws the five repeating along the chain: **Suppliers' Supplier → Supplier → Your Company → Customer → Customer's Customer**, with **Plan** sitting above and spanning further.

**Two features carry the meaning:** ① **the same five processes repeat at every link** — your *Deliver* is your customer's *Source*, which is what makes it a **reference model**; ② **Return is a first-class process**, because reverse logistics is a real and expensive flow.

*(The deck's own aside: "Have we seen this slide earlier? — **BPM!**" — SCOR is one of Unit 2's process-modelling standards.)*

items.q: SCM tracks three flows. In which directions do they move?
options: Material downstream, money upstream, information both ways
All three downstream, from supplier to customer
Material and money downstream, information upstream
Material upstream, money and information downstream
items.explain:
$$\textbf{goods flow down} \qquad \textbf{money flows up} \qquad \textbf{information flows both ways}$$

**Information is the one that can be improved almost for free, and that is the whole leverage of modern SCM.** Moving material faster costs money; **moving information faster costs almost nothing once systems are connected — and better information substitutes directly for inventory.**

**VMI replaces buffer stock with shared consumption data; CPFR replaces two forecasts with one; cross-docking replaces storage with synchronised schedules. Every one trades inventory for information.**

items.q: Which planning tools belong to the **strategic** level of supply chain planning?
options: Network Design and Long Term Planning (LTP)
S&OP, MPS and MRP
Detailed scheduling, transportation planning and route scheduling
Vendor schedules and distribution plans
items.explain:
**Strategic (yearly/quarterly)** — *"what is my long term capacity management strategy? what is my most optimized network design?"* → **Network Design, LTP**

**Tactical (monthly/weekly)** → **S&OP, MPS, MRP** · **Operational (daily/hourly)** → **detailed scheduling, transportation planning, route scheduling**

⚠️ **The whole MRP II ladder from Unit 3 sits inside *one* of SCM's three levels** — which is the implicit argument for why SCP exists. **MRP II has no strategic level at all.**

items.q: What separates strategic from tactical and operational decisions, beyond time horizon?
options: Reversibility — strategic decisions are "difficult to reverse without substantial cost for the change"
The number of people involved in making them
Whether they are made by software or by humans
Whether they affect revenue or only cost
items.explain:
The QnA gives it away for the strategic level, and it is the insight the exam wants.

| Level | Decision | Cost of changing your mind |
|---|---|---|
| **Strategic** | build a factory in Pune | **enormous** |
| **Tactical** | produce 8,000 units next month | moderate |
| **Operational** | send truck 4 via this route | **negligible** |

**Time horizon and reversibility go together for a physical reason: the longer the horizon, the more concrete the commitment.** A factory is bricks; a route is a line on a map.

items.q: In the SCP-versus-SCE table, the **Applications** row is asymmetric. What does it say, and why?
options: Planning: ERP or SCP solutions. Execution: ERP only — because execution must post to the ledger, respect authorisations and leave an audit trail
Planning: SCP only. Execution: ERP only — because they are entirely separate markets
Both rows say ERP — SCP solutions are only add-ons
Planning: ERP only. Execution: ERP or SCE solutions
items.explain:
$$\textbf{Planning: ERP } \textit{or} \textbf{ SCP solutions} \qquad \textbf{Execution: ERP } \textit{only}$$

> **Specialist planners exist; specialist executors do not.**

The deck's note names the reason: *"planning software need not worry about **access control, transaction management, workflow execution** — these are the must/should features of execution software such as ERP."*

**Same level-dependent conclusion as Unit 4's inventory pyramid:** the lower the level, the stronger the case for integrated ERP.

items.q: In the ERP-vs-SCP comparison, which row describes **SCP**?
options: Simultaneous planning of material and capacity, on finite capacity
Sequential planning of material and capacity, assuming infinite capacity
Cannot handle prioritization rules
Replanning takes a long time
items.explain:
**Every row of that table is one of MRP's seven limitations from Unit 3, answered:**

| MRP limitation | SCP row |
|---|---|
| *"assumes capacity is infinite"* | **finite capacity planning** |
| *"cannot consider constraints"* | **constraint based planning** |
| *"cannot do any optimization"* | **Advanced Planning and Optimization** |
| *"cannot replan fast enough"* | **replanning can be very quick** |

**MRP plans material first, then checks capacity — which is why closed-loop MRP loops back. SCP plans both in one pass, so the loop disappears because the constraint was inside the calculation from the start.**

items.q: In the deck's network-design trade-off, what were the two networks' savings and service levels?
options: Cost-optimal: $6m savings, 40% next day. Service-optimal: $3m savings, 80% next day
Cost-optimal: $3m savings, 80% next day. Service-optimal: $6m savings, 40% next day
Cost-optimal: $6m savings, 80% next day. Service-optimal: $3m savings, 40% next day
Both saved $6m at different service levels
items.explain:
$$\textbf{Doubling next-day service } (40\% \rightarrow 80\%) \textbf{ costs } \$3\text{m of the }\$6\text{m saving}$$

**There is no "right" answer between the two networks** — the cost-optimal network **consolidates into few large facilities**; the service-optimal one **spreads into many local ones**.

**Same trade-off as DRP's competing objectives, Level vs Chase, and service-level-based inventory. Four appearances of one structure.**

**What the optimiser provides is not the answer but the curve** — choosing a point on it is a business decision.

items.q: What is **"like modelling"** in demand planning, and what problem does it solve?
options: Forecasting a product with no history by borrowing the history of a similar one — it makes new-product planning possible
Grouping similar customers to forecast them together
Matching forecast shapes across regions
Using a competitor's sales as a proxy for your own
items.explain:
**A new phone model has no sales history; the previous model does.**

**Launch and phase-out are the two moments when history is the worst possible guide**, which is why both need their own capability — *"planning for new products"* and *"planning for Discontinuation / Phase out."*

⚠️ **Phase-out is the one people forget:** a forecast that extrapolates a dying product's history will **over-order right up to the end**, leaving exactly the obsolete stock the *inventory obsolescence* KPI measures.

*(SCM tools support like modelling; **ERP demand planning does not.**)*

items.q: Distinguish **consensus forecasting** from **collaborative forecasting**.
options: Consensus reconciles sales, marketing, finance and production inside one company; collaborative reconciles your forecast with your customer's, across companies
Consensus uses statistical models; collaborative uses expert judgement
Consensus is monthly; collaborative is weekly
They are two names for the same capability
items.explain:
**Consensus is S&OP's arbitration made into software** — Unit 3's *"joint plan developed by the Sales and Marketing team together."*

**Collaborative forecasting crosses the company boundary** — and is what becomes **CPFR**.

**Both are SCM-tool capabilities that ERP demand planning lacks:** *"does not support collaborative forecasting"* is an explicit row in the comparison table.

items.q: What is the difference between **available-to-promise (ATP)** and **capable-to-promise (CTP)**?
options: ATP asks whether stock or a planned receipt exists; CTP asks whether we could produce it in time, given components and capacity
ATP is for finished goods; CTP is for components
ATP is instantaneous; CTP runs overnight
ATP is an ERP feature; CTP is a manual process
items.explain:
$$\textbf{ATP: is there stock or a planned receipt?} \qquad \textbf{CTP: could we produce it?}$$

**CTP requires exactly what SCP has and ERP lacks — finite capacity and multi-level component visibility.** The deck calls it *"multi-level component **and capacity** check."* **You cannot promise to make something without knowing whether the machine is free.**

**GATP's six capabilities are an escalating search:** alternate location → alternate product → **capable-to-promise** → rule-based → calendars. **ERP's ATP looks up a number; GATP conducts a search.**

items.q: Match the transport optimisation area to its business need. Which pairing is **correct**?
options: Route optimization — minimize vehicle travel distance
Route optimization — minimize number of vehicles used
Optimum truck load building — minimize vehicle travel distance
Transport planning and vehicle scheduling — minimize unloading labour
items.explain:
$$\textbf{how many vehicles} \qquad \textbf{how far each travels} \qquad \textbf{how well each is packed}$$

- **Transport planning and vehicle scheduling** → **minimize number of vehicles used**
- **Route optimization** → **minimize vehicle travel distance**
- **Optimum truck load building** → **minimize unloading labour, and so the truck does not run empty**

**Load building and routing are coupled through drop sequence** — the last delivery is loaded first, deepest in the truck. **You cannot decide the packing until you know the route.**

items.q: Why does the deck call route optimization **"one of the most complex problems in computer science"**? *(select all that apply)*
options: It must respect vehicle capacity, distance/duration/stopover limits and drop sequence
It must respect stacking constraints — light materials must not sit below heavy ones
It must respect access restrictions such as border crossings allowed only at certain times
It requires real-time GPS tracking of every vehicle
items.explain:
It is the **vehicle routing problem** — a generalisation of the travelling salesman problem — and capacity, time windows, stacking rules and access restrictions make it dramatically harder.

⚠️ **The access-restriction example is the best illustration of why shortest-path alone is insufficient:** the shortest route may be **unusable at the hour the truck arrives**. **So the optimiser is scheduling in time, not just routing in space.**

*(Other constraints named: depot location, handling resources, maximum storage time, vehicle types, opening hours of locations.)*

items.q: The single most examinable fact about **VMI** is that the customer does **not** do what?
options: Generate a purchase order — the supplier drives replenishment and creates the order
Receive the goods — the supplier delivers straight to the shelf
Pay for the goods until they are sold
Hold any inventory at all
items.explain:
**"In VMI, the customer does not generate a P.O."** — that inverts the entire procurement cycle from Unit 4.

| | **Normal** | **VMI** |
|---|---|---|
| Who decides what to order | **customer** | **supplier** |
| What the customer sends | **a purchase order** | **stock, sales and promotion data** |

**Why it is better:** the supplier sees **actual consumption** rather than **a filtered order signal** distorted by the retailer's own batching and safety stock. **That is why "eliminating bullwhip effect" is the first benefit listed.**

*(The customer keeps a veto — *"review the order, if required make changes."*)*

items.q: Which are the **two stated difficulties** of VMI?
options: Unstable pricing / sudden demand surges are hard to handle, and VMI requires a critical volume of business
Suppliers resist it, and EDI standards are incompatible
It increases inventory, and it raises administration cost
It requires the same ERP at both ends, and it is illegal in some jurisdictions
items.explain:
**① VMI works by extrapolating consumption.** A price change or demand spike **breaks the extrapolation** — and because the customer is no longer ordering, **there is no signal that the world changed** except the data itself, arriving after the fact. *(Which is why **planned future promotions** is one of the three EDI feeds.)*

**② Setup costs both parties real integration effort.** The **saving is proportional to volume while the setup cost is fixed** — which is why VMI is a Wal-Mart-and-P&G story rather than a universal practice.

items.q: The collaboration evolution chart plots evolution against which vertical axis?
options: Collaboration / trust
Cost of integration
Number of trading partners
Data volume exchanged
items.explain:
$$\textbf{Paper based updates} \rightarrow \textbf{Portals} \rightarrow \textbf{Collaborative Forecasting, VMI} \rightarrow \textbf{CPFR}$$

**Technology was never the constraint — EDI existed for decades. Trust was.** A supplier who can see your daily sales can also infer your margins, your promotions and your relationships with their competitors.

The deck's own note: *"many of these may look trivial in the current age of on-line access… **but it was a big deal not too long ago.** Also, businesses won't embrace technology so quickly."*

items.q: What problem did **CPFR** originate to solve, per the deck?
options: That the company and their supplier do not work with the same forecast numbers
That suppliers were slow to deliver
That retailers held too much safety stock
That EDI formats were incompatible between trading partners
items.explain:
CPFR *"started as a vision for some of the large retailers like **Wal-Mart in the 1990s**, who found the biggest problem of supply chain is that **the company and their supplier do not work with the same forecast numbers**."*

**Both parties forecast the same future demand and get different answers, because each sees only part of the picture** — the retailer sees **actual sales**, the supplier sees **their own capacity**.

$$\textbf{two forecasts} \Rightarrow \textbf{two plans} \Rightarrow \textbf{one is wrong, and both pay}$$

**CPFR's answer is not a better algorithm — it is a *single* forecast.**

items.q: The **nine steps of CPFR** follow a repeating pattern. What is it?
options: Agree (2 steps), then create → identify exceptions → resolve exceptions TWICE (sales forecast, then order forecast), then generate order
Plan, do, check, act, repeated twice, then close
Three phases of three steps each: forecast, agree, replenish
Nine independent steps with no repeating structure
items.explain:
> ### **Agree, then forecast twice, then order.**

**Steps 3–5 and 6–8 are the same three steps applied to two different forecasts** — which is why nine steps are easier to remember than they look.

**Sales forecast = what the end consumer will buy. Order forecast = what the retailer will order from the supplier.** They are **not the same number** — a retailer selling 1,000/week may order 4,000 monthly. **The sales forecast is smooth; the order forecast is lumpy — and that gap is where the bullwhip is born.**

**VICS = Voluntary Intra Industry Commerce Standards.**

items.q: Four of CPFR's nine steps concern exceptions. Why do they matter so much?
options: Because the point of a joint forecast is that disagreement is detected and resolved before it becomes two different plans
Because exceptions are the only steps that can be automated
Because regulators require exception logging
Because they replace the need for a joint business plan
items.explain:
**An exception is a divergence beyond an agreed tolerance** — *your forecast says 1,200, mine says 800.*

> **Without steps 4–5 and 7–8, CPFR would just be two forecasts exchanged by email. The exception process is what makes it a single forecast.**

**Same discipline as MRP's exception messages** — *"prioritize the messages → take action"* — applied across a company boundary.

**And step 1 comes first for a reason:** *"develop collaboration arrangement"* is where the parties agree **what tolerance counts as an exception.**

items.q: Why does the **bullwhip effect** amplify as you move upstream? *(select all that apply)*
options: Order batching — a smooth demand becomes a spiky order
Safety stock adjustment — a 10% demand rise triggers a larger order increase
Each link can only see the orders from the link below it, not actual consumption
Upstream suppliers have longer production runs
items.explain:
Plus **lead-time reaction**, **promotions and forward buying**, and **shortage gaming**.

> **Every cause has the same root: each link sees only orders, not consumption.**

**Which is exactly why VMI eliminates it** — the supplier receives **POS data and stock levels**, not orders, so the distorting filter is removed. **And CPFR attacks it from the other side with a shared forecast.**

$$\textbf{small change in consumer demand} \xrightarrow{\text{each link amplifies}} \textbf{large swing at the manufacturer}$$

items.q: Name the **four characteristics** of a data warehouse.
options: Subject-oriented, integrated, time-variant, non-volatile
Normalized, indexed, partitioned, replicated
Structured, cleansed, consistent, current
Relational, dimensional, historical, secure
items.explain:
**Mnemonic: SITN** — and **each is a deliberate rejection of how an operational system works.**

| Characteristic | OLTP | Warehouse |
|---|---|---|
| **Subject-oriented** | organised by **process** | by **subject** — sales, product, customer |
| **Integrated** | one application | **many sources reconciled** |
| **Time-variant** | **current** state | **5–10 years** of history |
| **Non-volatile** | **updated constantly** | **write once, read many** |

**Non-volatile is the most important:** if a warehouse overwrote, **last year's report would silently change every time someone corrected a record today.**

items.q: What are the **two stated disadvantages** of data warehousing, and what causes each?
options: Data latency (caused by non-volatility and batch loading) and no unstructured data reporting (caused by the schema)
High cost and slow queries
Poor security and difficult administration
Vendor lock-in and licence cost
items.explain:
**Both follow directly from characteristics you were just told were advantages — and saying so is the mark-earning observation.**

$$\textbf{non-volatile + batch load} \Rightarrow \textbf{latency}$$

**Which is why an ODS exists** — *"a near real time integrated view of current data."*

**Unstructured data — emails, documents, images, call recordings, social media — does not fit facts-and-dimensions tables**, and it is exactly the data the CRM chapter said could be valuable.

*(Advantages: **common data model, clean data, better performance of source system, facilitates reporting**, plus storage over a longer period.)*

items.q: In the deck's worked star schema, the **SALES** fact table contains which columns?
options: Product_Code, Period_Code, Store_Code, Units_Sold, Dollars_Sold, Dollars_Cost
Product_Code, Description, Color, Size
Store_Code, Store_Name, City, Telephone, Manager
Period_Code, Year, Quarter, Month, Day
items.explain:
$$\textbf{fact table} = \textbf{foreign keys pointing outward} + \textbf{numbers to add up}$$

Options B, C and D are the three **dimension** tables — **PRODUCT, STORE and PERIOD**.

**The test:** **facts are things you would *add up*** (units, dollars); **dimensions are things you would *group by* or *filter on*** (product, month, store).

**Notice STORE contains Store_Name, Telephone, Manager** — descriptive and unaggregatable. **Putting them in the dimension keeps the fact table narrow, and a narrow fact table is a fast one at a billion rows.**

items.q: Why is the star schema **deliberately denormalised**?
options: Because warehouse data is non-volatile, so the reason for normalising (preventing update anomalies) evaporates — leaving only the benefit of avoiding joins
Because relational databases cannot enforce normalisation at scale
Because dimension tables are too small to normalise
Because OLAP servers require flat tables
items.explain:
| | **OLTP — normalized** | **Warehouse — star schema** |
|---|---|---|
| Goal | **avoid update anomalies** | **avoid joins** |
| Because | data changes constantly | **data is non-volatile** |

**Normalisation exists to prevent inconsistency when data is updated — and warehouse data is not updated. So you may trade storage for query speed freely.**

This is exactly what the OLTP/OLAP table says: *"OLTP database design is **highly normalized**… OLAP is **denormalized with limited tables**."* **The two designs are opposite because their workloads are opposite.**

items.q: In **ETL**, which step is described as doing the real work, and why?
options: Transform — it manufactures Integrated, Consistent, Subject-oriented and Time-variant from raw source data
Extract — because source systems are the hardest to read
Load — because target systems enforce constraints
All three equally
items.explain:
*"After extraction, the data need to be **transformed or modified depending on specific business logic** so that it can be sent to the target repository."*

| Transform does | Delivering |
|---|---|
| reconciling customer IDs across systems | **Integrated · Uniqueness** |
| standardising formats, units, currencies | **Consistency and Standardization** |
| restructuring process data into subjects | **Subject-oriented** |
| stamping records with a load date | **Time-variant** |

**Extract and Load are plumbing; Transform is where the warehouse's promises are kept.**

**Four usage areas:** data migrations · master data management · data warehousing and reporting · **compliance**.

items.q: Which characteristics belong to **OLAP** rather than OLTP? *(select all that apply)*
options: Database design is typically denormalized with limited tables
Data is consolidated for a period of time
Data reveals multi-dimensional views of business activities
Highly normalized, following ER diagrams and data modeling
items.explain:
**Option D is OLTP.** Its other characteristics: *manages ongoing transactional data* · *is the source of the data origin* · *involves RDBMS*.

**The whole comparison follows from one difference in workload:**

$$\textbf{OLTP: many users, tiny operations, constant writes} \qquad \textbf{OLAP: few users, huge queries, rare writes}$$

⚠️ **And OLAP characteristic ② states the dependency: *"OLAP database is formed from various databases which are OLTP in nature."*** **OLAP has no data of its own** — which is why latency is unavoidable.

items.q: Distinguish **slice** from **dice** in OLAP.
options: Slice fixes ONE dimension to one value; dice restricts SEVERAL dimensions to sub-ranges
Slice removes a dimension; dice adds one
Slice aggregates upward; dice drills downward
Slice is for time dimensions; dice is for all others
items.explain:
$$\textbf{A slice cuts one flat plane out of the cube; a dice cuts a smaller cube out of the cube.}$$

On the deck's CPG example — **Product** *(detergent, food, personal care, healthcare)* × **Sales Channel** *(retail, wholesale, export)* × **Regions** *(APAC, Americas, Europe)* — **"the Food slice"** fixes Product = Food. **A dice would take *food and personal care, in APAC and Europe, retail only*.**

**The five OLAP functionalities:** roll up/roll down · slice and dice · multidimensional data cube · **pivot** · sort.

items.q: Match the OLAP type to its storage approach. Which is **correct**?
options: HOLAP — summaries in a cube, detail left relational
ROLAP — data pre-aggregated into a multidimensional cube
MOLAP — data stays in relational tables, cubes computed on the fly
HOLAP — everything stored twice, in both forms
items.explain:
| Type | Storage | Trade-off |
|---|---|---|
| **ROLAP** — **Relational** | relational tables, cubes on the fly | **scales to huge volumes**, slower |
| **MOLAP** — **Multidimensional** | pre-aggregated cube | **very fast**, limited size |
| **HOLAP** — **Hybrid** | **summaries in a cube, detail relational** | fast at summary, drills to detail |

**HOLAP is the granularity trade-off implemented as an architecture** — the summarised side's speed and the detailed side's answerability, **both at once**.

items.q: An **ODS** reverses which characteristics of a data warehouse? *(select all that apply)*
options: Non-volatile — the ODS has an overwrite function (add, change, delete)
Time-variant — the ODS stores only very recent information
Subject-oriented — the ODS uses flat, transparent tables with no fact and dimension tables
Integrated — the ODS draws from a single source
items.explain:
⚠️ **Integrated is the one they SHARE** — *"an ODS consolidates data from multiple source systems."*

$$\textbf{Warehouse: "what has been happening over years?"} \qquad \textbf{ODS: "what is true right now, across all systems?"}$$

**The ODS is the answer to data latency**, the warehouse's stated disadvantage.

**"Overwrite function" is listed as an *advantage*** — the same property is a virtue or a defect depending on the question. **For history you must never overwrite; for current state you must.**

items.q: What are the **four properties** of a pattern identified by data mining?
options: Valid, novel, potentially useful, ultimately understandable
Accurate, complete, timely, unique
Significant, repeatable, measurable, actionable
Descriptive, predictive, prescriptive, diagnostic
items.explain:
**Each rules out a specific failure:** **valid** rules out statistical noise · **novel** rules out what you already knew · **potentially useful** rules out what you cannot act on · **understandable** rules out what nobody can interpret.

> **Novelty is what distinguishes mining from reporting: reporting answers questions you asked; mining finds patterns you did not know to ask about.**

⚠️ **Validity is the deck's own caution answered** — search a large dataset and you will find patterns by chance. **That is why "Results validation" is a named step** *(the three steps: **Data Preparation → Model Construction → Results validation**)*.

*(Option B is the **quality data** properties list.)*

items.q: What does **BI** add on top of OLAP, analytics and data mining?
options: Pushing rather than pulling — alerts, dashboards, scorecards, workflow and data delivery
Faster query execution on the same cubes
The ability to store unstructured data
Direct write-back to the source systems
items.explain:
$$\textbf{BI} \supset \{\textbf{OLAP}, \textbf{Analytics}, \textbf{Data Mining}, \textbf{Reporting}\}$$

**OLAP waits for someone to ask a question. Alerts, dashboards, scorecards, workflow and data delivery bring the answer to the person without them asking** — and route it onward when action is needed.

**That is the difference between a tool and a system:** *"correct problems **before** they affect customer satisfaction"* requires **being told**, not having to look.

**And the vendor list is an acquisition story:** **Business Objects → SAP · Cognos → IBM · Hyperion → Oracle.**

items.q: Which processes are named as **common across industries**? *(select all that apply)*
options: Financial and management accounting, corporate governance
HR processes — recruitment, payroll, talent management
Global trade — import procedure, documentation, customs
Oil exploration and product promotion
items.explain:
Plus **corporate services like travel management**, **quality management**, and **warehouse and transport management**.

⚠️ **Option D is the deck's own example of processes that DIFFER** — *"an oil and gas company needs **exploration**… that is not important for a consumer goods company. **Product promotion** is important for a consumer goods company… however that may not make any sense for a petroleum company where prices in countries like India are mostly dictated by government."*

$$\textbf{common} = \textbf{how a company runs itself} \qquad \textbf{specific} = \textbf{what the company actually does}$$

items.q: **Just in sequence (JIS)** deliveries, named as an automotive-specific process, differ from JIT how?
options: Parts arrive in the order the assembly line will use them, not merely at the right time
Parts arrive earlier, giving the line a buffer
Parts are delivered by the manufacturer rather than the supplier
Parts are sequenced by value rather than by need
items.explain:
$$\textbf{JIT: the right parts at the right time} \qquad \textbf{JIS: in the order the line will use them}$$

On a line building **multiple models mixed together**, the seats for car 47 must arrive **immediately before car 47 reaches the seat station** — not a pallet of assorted seats.

> **The supplier must sequence their delivery to your production sequence** — which requires them to see your line schedule in near real time. **That is the deepest possible supply-chain collaboration, beyond VMI and CPFR.**

items.q: **E-Pedigree**, a pharma-specific process, exists to defeat what?
options: Counterfeit medicines entering the legitimate supply chain
Patent infringement by generic manufacturers
Price gouging by distributors
Expired stock being resold
items.explain:
**An electronic record of every custody transfer a drug pack has undergone**, from manufacturer to pharmacy. **It is a legal requirement, not a business choice.**

> **That is batch management from Unit 3 taken to its logical end.** Batch tracking answered *"which batch is this?"*; **e-pedigree answers *"who has held this specific pack, and when?"*** — the same **Farm to Fork** traceability at pharmaceutical stakes.

**Every pharma process on the list exists because of regulation or intellectual property** — and *"secrecy of formulation"* is the one that constrains the ERP's own design.

items.q: Why does retail need **store clustering**?
options: Because per-store assortment planning is intractable at 800 stores and a single national assortment ignores real differences
Because stores must be grouped for tax purposes
Because POS systems can only serve one cluster at a time
Because warehouses serve stores in fixed groups
items.explain:
**Clustering groups similar stores so assortment and space decisions are made per cluster** — a few dozen decisions instead of 800.

> **Same "match the resolution to the decision" principle as ABC classification, rough-cut capacity planning and data granularity.**

**Retail's processes are all about *what to stock, where, and at what price*, because a retailer makes nothing** — category management, assortment management, space management, merchandise budgeting, promotion planning and markdowns.

items.q: In the healthcare provider's "Manage Resources" list, one entry is unlike any other inventory item. Which, and why?
options: Organs and blood — perishable in hours, non-substitutable, and impossible to reorder
Beds — because they cannot be moved between wards
Medications — because they require batch tracking
Operation theatres — because they are booked rather than stocked
items.explain:
**They have a stock level, a location, an expiry and a matching requirement** — but **no procurement lead time applies and no EOQ can be calculated.**

> **It is the extreme case of the critical-item quadrant — *"should never be out of stock"* — with no way to guarantee supply.**

**And the provider/payer split is the structural insight:** the provider's processes are **beds, theatres, tests, treatments**; the payer's are **claims, relationships, communication**. ***"Payer Relationship Management" is literally CRM where the customer is an insurer.***

items.q: Why do banking ERPs form a separate product category with their own vendors?
options: Because in a bank the financial transaction IS the product — there is no factory, the ledger is the operation
Because banking regulation forbids general-purpose ERP
Because banks require real-time processing that SAP cannot provide
Because banks do not need HR or procurement modules
items.explain:
**In a manufacturer, FI-CO *records* what production and sales did. In a bank, the financial transaction *is* the product.**

**Hence: Finacle (Infosys) · FLEXCUBE (Oracle) · IS-Banking (SAP) · BaNCS (TCS)** — two of the four Indian.

**Note that "Treasury management" appears here as a *core banking process*** while in Unit 3 it was one of four categories of the finance module for an ordinary company. **Same function, utterly different weight** — for a manufacturer treasury manages spare cash; **for a bank, interest rate, FX and credit risk management are the business.**

items.q: What is the deck's stated **criticism** of cloud computing?
options: Companies save on upfront capital but may pay more in operating expenses — so where capital expense is small, cloud may not make financial sense
Cloud providers cannot guarantee data residency
Cloud systems cannot scale beyond a certain user count
Cloud contracts always cost more than on-premise licences
items.explain:
**A genuine argument, not a hedge.** Cloud converts **CapEx into OpEx** — you stop buying hardware and start paying rent. **Rent never stops.**

> **Cloud wins where demand is variable or unpredictable; ownership wins where it is steady and large.**

**And the strongest advantage is stated as a full sentence:** *"individual companies need not design the hardware based on **peak load**."*

$$\textbf{on-premise capacity} = \textbf{peak demand} \qquad \textbf{cloud capacity} = \textbf{current demand}$$

items.q: Which SaaS characteristic generates all the others?
options: One-to-many delivery — one instance of the software serving many customers
Per-user subscription pricing
Network based access to business software
Central maintenance rather than at each customer site
items.explain:
$$\textbf{one instance of the software} \longrightarrow \textbf{many customers}$$

| Because it is one-to-many… | …this follows |
|---|---|
| maintenance happens once | **"managed from a central location"** |
| everyone is on the same version | **"faster releases — the whole community benefits"** |
| hardware is shared | **"multi-tenant efficiency — never idle"** |
| **you cannot change shared code** | **customization is impossible** |

**The last row is not a limitation of the technology — it is a direct consequence of the model.** Which is why *"SaaS became popular for applications that are more standard across industries."*

items.q: Which row of the **SaaS vs Hosted ERP** table describes **hosted ERP**?
options: Single tenant · licence fee · customer owns the licence · customization possible · customer decides upgrades
Multi tenant · subscription · vendor owns the licence · no customization · vendor decides upgrades
Multi tenant · licence fee · customer owns the licence · customization possible
Single tenant · subscription · vendor owns the licence · no customization
items.explain:
**All seven rows follow from row one — multi-tenant versus single-tenant.**

| Because SaaS is multi-tenant… | Because hosting is single-tenant… |
|---|---|
| **no customization** | **customization possible** — it is your instance |
| **vendor decides upgrades** | **customer decides**, or never upgrades |
| **vendor hosts and maintains** | **a service provider** hosts your copy |

⚠️ **The upgrade row has the sharpest consequence:** under SaaS you **cannot refuse an upgrade** — unsettling, but it also means **you can never fall into the *"customization ⇒ the system cannot evolve"* death spiral.**

items.q: Per the Panorama Consulting 2013 figures the deck cites, what share of ERP was still **on-premise**?
items.explain:
**On-Premise 61% · SaaS 14% · Cloud ERP 12% · Other 13%.** **The emerging trends were, at the time, genuinely emerging.**

**Why ERP resisted SaaS longer than CRM — three stated issues:** **security of customer specific data** · **ensuring high availability, as ERP is the heart of business operations** · **each customer needs specific customization, and it is difficult to stick to a standard solution.**

**The third is a contradiction, not a difficulty** — and the deck's resolution is *"offering **industry best-practice configurations** as well as the ability for the customer to do further **configuration**."* **Configuration, not code.**

items.q: Which are **SOA principles** per the deck? *(select all that apply)*
options: Re-usability and modularity
Composability, componentization and interoperability
Loose coupling and standards-compliance
Normalization and referential integrity
items.explain:
**Seven principles, three ideas:** *break it into pieces* (modularity, componentization) · *make the pieces fit* (composability, interoperability, standards-compliance) · *keep them independent* (loose coupling, re-usability).

**Loose coupling is load-bearing:** a service can be **changed or replaced without breaking its callers**, because they depend on its *interface*, not its internals.

**A service is defined as a business function:** *"each of these services is actually a business function"* — *check credit*, *create sales order* — which is why it is *"understood both by business executives and IT staff."*

items.q: What is described as **RFID's most talked about advantage** over bar codes?
options: It does not require line of sight between reader and tag
Tags are cheaper than printed labels
Tags are more durable in harsh environments
Readers are cheaper than laser scanners
items.explain:
**No line of sight means an entire pallet can be read as it passes through a doorway** — *"items kept deep inside boxes"* — instead of being unpacked and scanned one by one.

**The other two advantages:** tags hold **hundreds of characters vs 12–15 digits**; tags are **rewritable thousands of times** so data can be **added at each supply-chain node** — which is exactly what **e-pedigree** requires.

$$\textbf{bar code: an identifier} \qquad \textbf{RFID tag: a travelling record}$$

⚠️ **Disadvantages: standards immaturity (temporary) and tag cost (structural).**

items.q: For $n$ systems, how many interfaces does point-to-point integration require versus an EAI hub?
options: n(n−1)/2 for point-to-point; n for a hub
n for point-to-point; n(n−1)/2 for a hub
n² for point-to-point; 2n for a hub
Both require n interfaces; the hub is simply faster
items.explain:
| Systems | **Point-to-point** | **Hub** |
|---|---|---|
| 5 | **10** | **5** |
| 10 | **45** | **10** |
| 20 | **190** | **20** |

**The gap widens quadratically**, and maintenance widens with it: in point-to-point, **changing one system's format means changing every interface that touches it.**

**EAI is what makes ERP II possible** — *"ERPs now can be integrated with best-of-breed vendors seamlessly **with one interface**"* is a named driver, and *"with one interface"* is precisely the hub model.

items.q: What are the **three major drivers** for the journey from ERP to ERP II?
options: ERPs extending outside the organization · accessible anywhere anytime · integrable with best-of-breed vendors with one interface
Falling hardware costs · rising licence fees · shorter implementation times
Regulatory pressure · globalisation · consolidation of vendors
Better forecasting · finite capacity planning · optimization algorithms
items.explain:
**The three drivers are the three technologies of the topic, one each:**

| Driver | Technology |
|---|---|
| **extending outside the organization** | **SOA and web services** |
| **accessed from anywhere anytime** | **mobile, internet, cloud** |
| **integrated with best-of-breed, one interface** | **EAI** |

$$\textbf{ERP: internal resource optimization} \longrightarrow \textbf{ERP II: process integration and external collaboration}$$

**"Collaborative commerce with suppliers and customers is the heart of ERP II"** — and this unit showed exactly what that means: **VMI and CPFR** with suppliers, **CRM and e-commerce** with customers, **SCM** across the network, **DW-BI** to understand it.
